source.title: From Directions to Cones: Exploring Multidimensional Representations of Propositional Facts in LLMs
source.authors: Stanley Yu; Vaidehi Bulusu; Oscar Yasunaga; Clayton S. Lau; Cole Blondin; Sean O'Brien; Kevin Zhu; Vasu Sharma

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports an exploratory ablation of a toxicity difference-in-means direction and its effects on refusal-related outputs, using a different target and setup from the original refusal-direction test.
record.gate_note: The paper's main experiments concern truth directions and truth concept cones, not refusal, so those results are not recorded here. Appendix B.2 reports the relevant toxicity-direction ablations. Values used to construct or select directions are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper borrows the refusal-direction toolkit (DIM directions, directional ablation, concept cones) and applies it to propositional truth. It reports only truth-steering results. Its one refusal-adjacent result (Appendix B.2) ablates a toxicity DIM direction built from toxic vs benign phrases, not a harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction. That result is a single qualitative sentence with no model named and no rate of refusal, so it tests no version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase of Appendix B.2 is accurate. However, the paper's main conclusion should be stated. Multi-dimensional concept cones (up to 5D) causally mediate Yes/No answers on simple true/false propositions in Qwen2.5 and Gemma-2 instruct models, with low KL divergence on Alpaca. Only the first cone axis aligns with the truth DIM direction. The authors draw no conclusion about refusal.
record.recipe_differences: The reported experiment uses toxicity-related directions and toxic-output behavior, rather than the original harmful-versus-harmless instruction direction and refusal intervention.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating a toxicity DIM direction (ToxiGen) removed explicit refusal phrasing, but the model still declined to produce toxic output. Unnamed model, qualitative only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A toxicity-content direction may control refusal phrasing without controlling avoidance of toxic generation.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating a student–teacher activation-difference direction for toxicity produced unintelligible output.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Student–teacher difference directions for toxicity do not give clean ablation interventions.

record.code_released: All code will be open-sourced on Github; URL not stated.
record.problems: The Appendix B.2 toxicity results do not identify the specific models, give quantitative measures, or report uncertainty. The student–teacher direction produced unintelligible output, and the authors say they could not obtain a valid linear direction for toxicity.
record.rows_left_out: Results on truth directions, truth cones, and general-capability retention were left out because they do not test the refusal claim.
record.verdict_notes: The main results concern truth cones and do not bear on the refusal-direction claim; they are analogous in method only. The record's V5 'supports' label is removed. The toxicity direction is not a harmfulness-judgment representation, and the result is unquantified and from an unnamed model. The study is reclassified from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test a harmful-minus-harmless instruction refusal direction, its ablation across layers and positions, addition of that direction, or preservation of general capabilities under those refusal interventions.
No weight-edit or abliteration result is reported.
No jailbreak suppression of a refusal direction or training against its ablation is tested.
The paper's multidimensional-cone results concern truth representations, not whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or carried by multiple directions.

The paper reports refusal-related behavior after toxicity-direction ablation, but does not directly measure a harmfulness judgment or establish separate internal representations for judgment and refusal.
No transfer of a refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models is tested.
No comparison of refusal training methods or training stages is reported.
No reasoning-model refusal-direction test is reported.

rows.subject: model not stated
rows.operation_detail: Ablated the difference-in-means direction computed for toxicity.
rows.measure: Explicit refusal phrasing and refusal to generate toxic output
rows.value: Strong explicit refusal was disabled, but the model still refused to generate toxic output.
rows.note: The text does not name the model or quantify either behavior. This is evidence of a behavioral dissociation after ablation, but it does not directly measure an internal harmfulness judgment.
rows.check: The direction is a toxicity DIM computed from ToxiGen phrases, not a refusal or harmfulness-judgment direction. The text does not name the model and gives no refusal rate or baseline. The outcome (no 'I cannot respond', yet still declines toxic output) is anecdotal and does not measure an internal harm judgment separate from refusal, so it cannot bear on V5. The authors themselves say they failed to obtain a valid toxicity direction.

rows.subject: student model and teacher model; specific models not stated
rows.stage_stated: typically instruction-tuned; exact stage not stated
rows.operation_detail: Ablated a direction formed from the activation difference between a student and teacher model.
rows.note: The reported outcome does not establish a refusal or harmfulness-judgment effect.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. The student–teacher direction ablation gave unintelligible output and reports no refusal measure.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The reported difference between loss of strong explicit refusal and continued refusal to generate toxic output is consistent with a distinction between refusal expression and toxic-content avoidance (r1); the study does not directly test the internal judgment representation.
